title: Dangun and the Bear Woman
source_ref: Samguk Yusa (1281), book 1 ('Giyi'), drawing on older records
paragraphs: Hwanung, son of Hwanin, lord of heaven, looked down on the world and asked to rule it. His father sent him to earth with three thousand followers. He descended at Taebaek Mountain, under a sandalwood tree, and brought wind, rain, clouds, grain and laws. There he governed the affairs of people.

A bear and a tiger came to him and asked to become human. Hwanung gave them a bundle of mugwort and twenty cloves of garlic, and told them to eat nothing else and stay out of sunlight for one hundred days. The tiger soon gave up and left. The bear endured to the end, and became a woman.

Ungnyeo, the bear woman, was grateful. She prayed beneath the sandalwood tree for a child, and Hwanung answered her. In one telling he took human form for a time and married her; in another he simply granted her wish. She bore a son, Dangun Wanggeom, and raised him in the mountain country.

Dangun founded Gojoseon, the first Korean kingdom, with its capital at Asadal, near modern Pyongyang. Tradition dates the founding to 2333 BCE. The Samguk Yusa, compiled in 1281, is the earliest surviving text to tell the story in full, and it drew on older records that no longer exist. Historians treat the date and the king as legendary, while many Koreans honour them as origins.
notes: The Samguk Yusa is the earliest full narrative, compiled more than a millennium after the traditional date. The bear-woman episode, the length of the test and Hwanung's marriage to Ungnyeo vary in later retellings, and the date 2333 BCE is traditional rather than archaeological.

title: Jumong and the Sun
source_ref: Samguk Sagi (1145) and Samguk Yusa (1281), Goguryeo foundation accounts
paragraphs: Yuhwa was the daughter of Habaek, the god of the Amnok River. One day she met Hae Mosu, a son of heaven who had come down to earth, and she conceived. Her father, ashamed and angry, expelled her from the river court. She came to the land of Buyeo, where King Geumwa found her and gave her shelter.

In Buyeo the sources diverge. The Samguk Sagi says Yuhwa had already conceived by Hae Mosu; later tellings say that sunlight followed her into the palace and made her pregnant there. Either way, heaven is named as the child's origin. She gave birth to a large egg. The court called it a curse, and Geumwa had it exposed, but animals and birds protected it.

The egg hatched a boy. He was named Jumong, a Buyeo word for a skilled archer, and he grew up strong and quick. When he shot, he rarely missed. Geumwa's sons grew jealous of him, and the court turned against the boy who had hatched from an egg. Jumong left Buyeo with three companions and went south.

In the south, Jumong reached Jolbon and founded Goguryeo in 37 BCE. He became its first king, and the state he made lasted for centuries. The Samguk Sagi, completed in 1145, and the Samguk Yusa, completed in 1281, preserve his story, each shaped by the politics of its own time. Yuhwa was later honoured as a goddess of the cave, and her son as a divine king.
notes: The identity of Jumong's father is told in two ways: the Samguk Sagi names Hae Mosu, a heavenly man, while other accounts emphasise a sunbeam that makes Yuhwa pregnant in Buyeo. The egg birth and the 37 BCE founding date are traditional, and the sources were written centuries after the events they describe.

title: Princess Bari
source_ref: Korean shamanic narrative (muga), performed in gut rituals; regional versions differ
paragraphs: A king and queen had six daughters and longed for a son. Their seventh child was another girl. The king, furious, ordered the baby sealed in a jade box and cast into the sea. In some regions she is left on a mountain instead. The child survived. A poor couple found the box and raised her, naming her Bari, which means the discarded one.

Years later, the king fell ill. No doctor could cure him, and the shamans said that only the water of life, kept in the Western Paradise beyond death, could save him. He summoned his six remaining daughters. One by one they refused the journey. Then he learned that the child he had thrown away was still alive, and he sent for her.

Bari agreed to go. She crossed rivers and mountains of the underworld, passed the guardians of each threshold with offerings rather than force, and reached the Western Paradise. Its guardian, Mujangseung, would not give up the water. She served him for years, carried water, cut wood and tended his fire. In many tellings she became his wife and bore him seven sons before he let her take the water.

She returned to find her father already dead. She poured the water of life over him, and he revived. Offered the kingdom, she refused it and chose instead to guide the souls of the dead. In the shamanic narrative she becomes the first mudang, and the ssitgim-gut, a ritual for the dead, re-enacts her journey. Versions differ sharply by region.
notes: This retelling follows one widely performed version of the muga, in which Bari is set adrift in a jade box, serves Mujangseung and revives her dead father. Jeju, Seoul and other regional traditions tell the story differently, and some versions make Bari the goddess of the dead rather than the first shaman.

title: The Woodcutter and the Heavenly Maiden
source_ref: Korean oral folktale (ATU 400), collected in many regional variants
paragraphs: A poor woodcutter lived at the foot of Diamond Mountain with his mother. One day he saved a deer from a hunter, and the deer, grateful, told him a secret. High on the mountain were pools where heavenly maidens came down to bathe. If he hid one maiden's robe, the deer said, she could not fly home, and she would become his wife.

The woodcutter climbed to the pools and waited. The maidens descended on a rainbow, left their robes by a pine tree and entered the water. He took the youngest one's robe and hid. When the others flew away, she remained, stranded. He comforted her and led her down the mountain. They married, and in time she bore him children.

For years he kept the robe hidden. The maiden missed the sky. At last, after the birth of their third child, she found the robe and put it on. She rose into the air, taking the children with her. The woodcutter grieved. The deer told him to wait by the pools, where a gourd, a bucket or a rope ladder would be let down from heaven. He climbed in and was drawn up.

In heaven his wife's father, the Heavenly King, received him, and for a time the family was happy. But the woodcutter missed his mother. He returned to earth on a heavenly horse, was warned not to dismount, and dismounted anyway. The horse flew back without him. In many versions he grieves until he becomes a rooster, crowing at dawn for the sky. Other versions end with reunion, or with tasks in heaven.
notes: The tale is classified as ATU 400 and survives in many Korean versions. The ascent may be by a rope, a gourd, a bucket or a vine ladder; the ending may be reunion, a heavenly test, or the woodcutter's transformation into a rooster. This retelling combines the most commonly collected motifs. Modern retellings often comment on the coercive premise of the stolen robe.

title: The Rabbit and the Dragon King
source_ref: Korean oral folktale, also performed in the pansori repertory as Sugungga
paragraphs: The Dragon King of the sea fell ill. His physicians said that only a rabbit's liver could cure him, but no rabbit lived under the water. The court searched for a volunteer. A turtle offered to swim to the shore, find a rabbit and bring it back. He crawled onto the beach and began to praise the wonders of the sea palace.

A rabbit listened. The turtle described gardens of coral, food without work and a king who rewarded visitors. The rabbit, curious and hungry, climbed onto the turtle's shell, and they set off. As the water closed over them, the turtle admitted the truth: the rabbit was going to be killed, and its liver cut out for the king.

The rabbit's heart sank, but he kept his voice calm. 'Why did you not say so at once?' he asked. 'I keep my liver outside my body. I washed it this morning and hung it on a tree in the hills. If the king needs it, we must go back and fetch it.' The turtle turned around.

On the shore the rabbit leapt from the shell and ran. From a safe distance he laughed at the turtle, and at the king who thought a liver could be borrowed like a coat. The turtle returned alone. The tale is told for laughs, and it mocks both the powerful who demand the impossible and the clever who survive by talking.

title: Sim Cheong
source_ref: Korean folktale and the pansori Simcheongga, extant versions from the 18th century onward
paragraphs: Sim Cheong lived in a village with her blind father, Sim Bongsa. Her mother had died giving birth to her. The two were poor, and Cheong cared for her father with patience. A monk told Bongsa that if he gave three hundred sacks of rice to the temple, he would see again. Bongsa promised, but he had no rice.

Sailors came to the village looking for a girl to offer to the sea, so that their ship might pass safely. They would pay three hundred sacks of rice. Cheong heard, and offered herself. She said goodbye to her father and stepped onto the ship. At Indangsu, the dangerous water, she threw herself into the sea.

She did not drown. The Dragon King of the sea received her in his palace and treated her as a daughter. In some tellings she becomes queen of the underwater realm. In the best-known version she returns to the surface inside a great lotus flower, and a king finds the flower and makes her his queen.

As queen, she invited the blind beggars of the kingdom to a banquet. Her father came, still blind and still searching for her. When she spoke his name, he recognised her voice. His sight returned, and in the pansori every blind guest at the feast sees again. The story ends in rejoicing. It exists in many versions, and Simcheongga is one of the five surviving pansori.
notes: Sim Cheong's tale survives in oral versions, in the pansori Simcheongga and in printed novels. Details vary: the sea sacrifice, the Dragon King's treatment of her, the lotus flower, and whether she becomes a queen on land or under the sea. This retelling follows the pansori outline.
